newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Expectation low as Horn and Meciar prepare to meet. [CORRECTED 16:50 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Expectation low as Horn and Meciar prepare to meet. [CORRECTED 16:50 GMT]

text.p: The prime ministers of Slovakia and Hungary, preparing to meet on Friday, will attempt to ease recent tensions caused because Slovakia was not invited to talks on NATO and EU accession and Bratislava's treatment of Slovakia's ethnic Hungarian minority.

Both governments have said the meeting between Gyula Horn and Vladimir Meciarin the west Hungarian town of Gyor will have no fixed agenda, allowing the discussion of any issue either leader wishes to raise.
"One could say nothing is excluded," said adviser to Horn Tamas Horvath. "It is in the nature of such meetings."

Relations between the two governments have been cool mainly as a result of Slovakia's policy towards its 500,000-strong Hungarian minority and a prolonged legal dispute over the diversion of the Danube by Bratislava to feed a $1 billion hydro-electric project at Gabcikovo.

The project had been planned jointly by Czechoslovakia and Hungary, but just before the new state of Slovakia took over the project at the end of 1992, Hungary pulled out, citing environmental reasons.

Slovakia pushed on with its plan to divert the Danube, which forms the border between the two countries, provoking protests by Hungary and a decision by both countries to take the case to the International Court at the Hague, which is currently deliberating on the matter.

A further potential division has arisen with NATO's invitation in July for Hungary to be in the first group of former communist countries to join the Western alliance, followed swiftly by the European Commission's recommendation that Hungary join four other east European states in early talks on European Union membership.
Slovakia, once seen as a frontrunner to join both groups, was in neither list of potential new members.
Slovak government spokeswoman Magda Pospisilova said Bratislava expected Hungary to "disclose its integration plans" following the two invitations.
The last formal meeting between Meciar and Horn was in early 1995 in Paris when they signed a friendship treaty under the auspices (and pressure) of the European Union.
Hungary ratified the treaty that summer but it took the Slovaks more than a year, with numerous postponements, to ratify it.

Hungary complains that Bratislava has still to put into practice many of its provisions, notably on the use of the mother tongue by its Hungarian minority and the setting-up joint implementation committees which would include members of all ethnic minorities.
Horn earlier this week described agreement on implementation of the treaty as a key task of the summit.

Two of Hungary's main opposition parties said on Thursday they expected nothing from the meeting while the parliamentary leader of Horn's coalition partners said no agreements are likely to come out of the meeting.
But Laszlo Valki, a professor of international law who headed Hungary's team of experts at the Hague hearings, said Horn believes that talking to Meciar is still the best approach.
"He always convinced that if there are conflicts you have to negotiate, negotiate, negotiate," he said. "And as such he can't really lose because expectations are so low."
